div.head: Chapter 26
div.p: From the moment they set foot on that land — and above all from the moment those hundred and seventy false apostles seized King Atahualpa — the right of continual and just war against all the Spaniards, as against public enemies of the human race, was acquired by the children and heirs of the said King Atahualpa and by all the peoples of those kingdoms. And this right to wage just war against all the Spaniards endures perpetually until the day of judgment, unless it is interrupted by one of four means: either by peace, or by truce, or by possible satisfaction made by the Spaniards to the aggrieved parties; or by remission that those who received the wrongs make of their own free and spontaneous will, without force or fear — provided that the infliction of injuries, tyranny, and oppression ceases, which without interruption all the lords who are still alive and all the peoples now endure.

It was said "from the moment they set foot on that land" because merely to disembark without license on another's land or kingdom — especially with armed men — is said to disturb the kingdom and its lord and to commit injury against him, as appears from the laws ff. e injuriarum, § si quis me prohibeat et §. fina. et. l. sane. et l. is qui in domum alienam, etc.

Or if it is preferred to state it in Latin, thus: From the moment those hundred and seventy false apostles invaded that land — and above all from the moment they seized the aforesaid King Atahualpa in bonds — the right was acquired of declaring just war against all the Spaniards as public enemies of the human race, in favor of the children and heirs of the named king and likewise of all the peoples of those kingdoms. Which right of declaring just war against us all is continuous and will be perpetual until the day of judgment, unless it is interrupted by some one of four resolutions: namely, by peace, or by truce, or by satisfaction on the part of the aggressors, or by remission that is entirely voluntary and spontaneous, without force or fear, on the part of the injured parties; provided nonetheless that the inflicting of injuries and harms ceases, and the imposing of tyranny or oppression by which all the petty kings and princes, or lords, and all the peoples are presently afflicted without respite.

The conclusion is proved in multiple ways. But first let it be known that, as was said in the second principle, § 2: a just war is any war declared for the cause of defense, or for the cause of coercing or repelling evil men, lest they inflict injuries or harms on those who do not offend them, or for the cause of recovering things that were seized, or for the cause of compensating for lesions or harms inflicted, or for the cause of avenging injuries received, or for the cause of necessity, to acquire or defend peace and liberty, as in c. apud vero Dei cultores, 23, q. 1, et c. Nolí.

The first cause is plain from L. ut vim, ff., De iustitia et jure, et in c. dilectio, De sententia excommunicationis, Lib. 6, where it says: "Since all laws and all rights permit force to be repelled by force, and allow all to defend themselves" et in c. significasti, the 22nd, De homicidio. The natural reason for this defense is that every substance naturally desires its own preservation according to its nature, according to Saint Thomas, 1.2 q. 94 a. 2 corp. and book 3, chapter 3, Contra gentiles, where he says "that all natural agents, insofar as they have power, resist corruption to the same degree, which is the evil by which each thing cannot be preserved in its own being but is corrupted." We see by experience that a stone, through its own hardness which is its power, resists as much as it can everything that seeks to break or corrupt it. "Now things that are hard, like stones, cling with most tenacious bonds to their parts; and in order not to be easily dissolved, they resist." And further on: "But nature works for each thing what is fitting to it, so that, as long as they can, they may not perish but remain." Thus Boethius, book 3, prose 11.

And if for all created things, even insensible ones, the appetite to preserve their being and to resist as much as they can everything contrary that can corrupt them is natural — which is nothing other than self-defense —: how much more must this be, and is it, natural to men, who surpass all others in dignity and excellence, to defend their being, whether natural being or political being.
Therefore just is the war moved by any private person, or by an entire people or kingdom, for the cause of its defense.

The second cause, for coercion and resistance against evil and harmful men who wish to commit injury or harm against those who never offended them. And this is nearly the same as the cause of natural defense. Of it the first chapter, 23, q. 2, makes mention there: "War is just when carried out for the purpose of repelling evils."

The third is to recover what was unjustly robbed, or to compensate for the evils and harms received: of which the said first chapter, and the following chapter Dominus noster, and the first chapter: "War is just when it is waged by edict to recover one's own property, etc."

The fourth is to punish and chastise injuries and harms received, and of it the said chapter Dominus noster also makes mention: "Just wars are commonly defined, he says, as those that avenge injuries: if any nation or city must be sought out or punished because it has neglected to punish what its subjects did wrongly, or to return what was taken away by injury." Thus far there.

This established, the first part of the conclusion is proved thus: most just and right is the war that one people or kingdom has against another in which all four causes of just war concur. Now in the right that the peoples of Peru have — from the moment they seized King Atahualpa — against the Spaniards, all four causes concur. Therefore the most just war, or the right to declare it, is what they have against them. Of the first proposition no one doubts, because if by even a single one of the said causes just war can be waged: it will be far more just where all four concur. The second proposition is proved — namely, that all four causes concur in the right that the peoples of those kingdoms have against us. That the first, which is defense — which extends to nearly all of them — concurs, appears thus: because those first Spaniards entered those kingdoms killing, seizing, destroying, robbing, and subjugating without any cause, as the proper and true tyrants they were: as was proved in the first principle and in the second, § 4, and in principle 7, and in the first conclusion, § 23. For against the onslaught of any tyrants and invaders of foreign kingdoms and killers of men who had done them no harm or wrong, defense and resistance are the remedy — no one is ignorant of this. Therefore those peoples had the most just cause and a war of just defense against those men and the rest of our nation who subsequently joined them.

The second, by reason of coercion and resistance — which is the same as the preceding —: who can deny that they had the right to coerce and resist and impede from doing further harm those who with such furious, blind, cruel, and brutish fury, so entirely without cause, were tearing apart and killing and robbing peoples who were in their own lands, without going to or harming those of others? Therefore they also had just cause by reason of coercion and of preventing from advancing further such great devastations and irreparable harms: to wage war against us.

The third, to recover and compensate for the evils and harms received: will there be any man in the world who has sense who will not confess and affirm that they had more than sufficient right to wage war against us? To have seized their king and lord and held him prisoner and in the end burned him alive would be cause enough for those kingdoms to take up arms for his liberation, and after his death to take satisfaction for his death and for the seven or eight thousand they tore apart there, and for those they had killed in the towns of Coaque and on the island of Puná, and everywhere they passed until they arrived at Cajamarca where they seized the king. Would it have been an unjust cause to wage war against those who had robbed them of such great treasures and robbed them more each day? Would it have been just cause for war and to die in war to recover the kingdoms and lordships that they usurped and had usurped from that supreme king and from many great lords? Would it have been just war to recover their liberty, seeing themselves subjected to so fierce a people, and at first sight so ferocious and cruel, armed with such heavy weapons, from which they could well know and foresee what they were going to be reduced to in time? Of this last cause Cicero says in the Philippics 7: "There is no more just cause of war than to repel servitude. Whence among the Romans the fight was first for the liberty of the city, then for dominion," as Policraticus, book 8, chapter 5 says; and Sallust in the Catilinarian: "No good man loses his liberty except together with his life."

To free the said king from imprisonment before they killed him, his children and his peoples were bound to make war upon us to liberate him, and it would have been most just by natural law. This appears first from the war Abraham made against the four kings who took his nephew Lot prisoner, along with the women and children and all his substance, as is read in Genesis, chapter 14. Second, from the fidelity that peoples swear to their kings — and even without swearing it they owe it by natural law — by which subjects are far more obliged to liberate and aid their king in any extremity, even at the risk of their lives, than they are to their relatives, even their parents. For the king is the head of the whole mystical body that is the kingdom and commonwealth, for the sake of the common good, which is the more divine according to the Philosopher, 1 Ethicorum, and each person is born more for this common good than for his father, who is a particular thing: "whence it is said that a man is born more for his country than for his father." And for this reason the law says: "That the defense without the discipline of the camp was more ancient for Roman citizens and fathers than affection for their children": L. postliminium, § filius, ff., De captivis et postliminiis. Each one is born for his country, as in L. 1, § Generaliter, ff., De ventre in possessionem mittendo. And it is lawful to kill parents, and conversely, those who come to destroy the fatherland, L. minime, ff., De religiosis et sumptibus funerum; pertinent is L. omne, final, ff., De re militari. From this it follows that every subject, to the extent his strength allows, is bound not to abandon his king in his adversities, to guard and defend him as the head of all the fatherland and commonwealth, even at the risk of his own life and of his wife and children; for we see that nature teaches this: because reason imitates nature, the arm and the hand expose themselves to being cut off and lost to save the head as the most principal member, and from whose loss the greatest harm would come to the whole body; and the analogy from the natural body to the mystical body is a good one, as in L. Adoptio, ff., De adoptione et in cap. qui plerique, De officio ordinarii, etc.

And not only are subjects bound to expose and risk their lives for the person of their king, the mystical head: but also for the recovery of his state and dignity and jurisdiction and his goods and royal rights. For the same reasons: and because without temporal goods — and especially if the state and dignity and jurisdiction and the royal rights are lacking — a king cannot be a king nor sustain himself for the governance and benefit of the whole mystical body, which is the kingdom and community of which he is the head: an argument drawn from the ley necare, ff., De liberis cognoscendis, and from what the gloss notes in L. quisquis, § penúlt., Codex, De donationibus.
